column4: The tree from Mount Sinai produces oil and a relish for eaters; it uniquely joins the surah's olive, its food and oil uses, and the adjacent Mount.
The light parable names a blessed olive tree and oil that almost shines before fire touches it, developing the section's non-food use of pressed olive oil.
At the promised meeting by the right side of the Mount, God sends down manna and quails, exactly joining the section's Tur setting to its heavenly food sense of م ن ن.
The Israelites are shaded, given manna and quails, and told to eat the good things provided to them; this is the named heavenly-food branch of م ن ن.
In the wilderness provision scene, water, shade, manna, quails, and the command to eat good provision occur together.
Belief and good works receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, an exact parallel to the section's unceasing wage.
The exception for believers who do good ends with أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, repeating both the condition and reward of 95:6.
The Prophet is promised أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ, preserving the section's phrase for reward that is never cut off.
Property is called قِيَامًا and its holders must provide food and clothing from it, directly realizing the dictionary sense of sustenance that keeps people standing.
God makes the Kaaba and sacred rites قِيَامًا لِلنَّاسِ; this is the wording behind the section's claim that the sacred center sustains people's worldly life and return.
Abraham asks that the town be secure and that its people be provided with fruits, exactly uniting the safe city and fruit-rizq.
Abraham asks for fruit provision for his family in an uncultivated valley beside the Sacred House so that they may give thanks.
A secure sanctuary to which the fruits of every kind are gathered is presented as provision from God.
The Lord of the House feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear, the same food-and-safety pairing developed by the section.
Rain-grown vegetation includes olive and pomegranate, and the hearer is told to look at fruit as it forms and ripens.
Olive and pomegranate stand among cultivated produce, followed by commands to eat their fruit and give its due at harvest.
Rain is the means by which God grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit for people.
The command that the human being look at his food opens the very food sequence in which the section locates the olive.
Olive and palm are explicitly items in the food catalogue begun by the command to look at one's food.
Pilgrims are told to take provisions for the journey and then that the best provision is mindfulness, extending material travel-food toward a nonmaterial provision as the section does.
Jesus asks for a table sent from heaven as a feast and sign, and calls God the best provider; it joins the section's table image with food descending from above.
After famine comes a year of rain in which people press produce, supplying the Quran's clearest counterpart to the olive press evoked by the section.
Those who do not follow spending with مَنّ or injury have their reward with their Lord, joining the reproach sense of the root to a reward left unspoiled by it.
The blessed are given عَطَاءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ, a gift explicitly not cut off and thus a close semantic counterpart to inexhaustible reward.
Paradise is called God's provision and is said to have no depletion, stating directly the section's reading of unending reward as inexhaustible rizq.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, and patient deeds receive their reward; this states the temporal boundary behind the uncut wage.
The promised garden has enduring fruit and shade, making lasting fruit itself an image of provision that does not cease.
Abundant fruit is one item of the provision of the companions of the right.
That fruit is neither cut off nor withheld, making fruit the direct form of the section's uninterrupted provision.
The righteous are repeatedly provided fruit in the gardens and recognize it as provision, directly joining fruit to recompense.
The sincere servants are promised a known provision, which the next ayah specifies as fruits.
Fruits are the named form of the honored provision promised in the preceding ayah.
God sends rain and thereby brings out fruits as provision, stating the causal line that the olive-growth passages exemplify.
Rainwater produces palm-and-grape gardens with many fruits to eat, immediately before the Sinai oil tree.
The fruits of palms and vines yield both an intoxicant and good provision, another case of fruit being processed into distinct human uses.
Immediately after the manna and Mount scene, the recipients are told to eat the good things provided and not transgress in them.
After the parable of lost security and abundance, people are told to eat lawful good provision and thank God's favor.
In the continuation of the olive-light passage, God rewards deeds and gives provision without account, bringing light, reward, and boundless provision into one context.
The steadfast are paid their reward without account, a close formulation of reward without a limiting measure.
The righteous enter the Garden and are provided there without account, explicitly construing eschatological reward as unlimited provision.
Provision and what is promised are said to be in heaven, directly illuminating the section's heavenly food and promised wage.
People are commanded to seek provision from God, worship and thank Him, and are reminded that they return to Him; worldly maintenance and return are held together.
People are told to travel through the made-manageable earth, eat God's provision, and remember resurrection to Him, closely joining journey-food, livelihood, and return.
People eat the fruit of the gardens while being reminded that their hands did not create it and asked whether they will give thanks.
The rain-grown grain and palms are provision for servants, and the same scene turns to resurrection from dead land.
Saba's two gardens accompany the command to eat the Lord's provision and give thanks in a good land.
God gives the earth as settlement, forms human beings well, and provides good things, bringing excellent human formation and sustenance into one ayah.
Human dignity, carriage over land and sea, and provision from good things occur together, linking the honored human form with sustaining gifts.
A secure, tranquil town receiving abundant provision from every place denies God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear; this is the section's central reversal in full.
The recipients of manna reject one food and ask for earth-grown vegetables, exchanging what is better for what is lower; it exposes ingratitude within the heavenly-food scene.
When Saba turns away, its two fruitful gardens are replaced by bitter produce, directly reversing the provision and gratitude of 34:15.
The passing bloom of worldly life is set against the Lord's provision, which is better and more lasting.
Fear, hunger, and loss of wealth and fruits are named as trials, forming the precise negative boundary of secure fruit-abundance.
Pharaoh's people are seized with years of drought and shortage of fruits so that they might take heed.
A secure sanctuary amid people being snatched away is followed by the charge that its inhabitants deny God's favor.
Faith and mindfulness would open blessings from heaven and earth, while denial turns that abundance into seizure.
Gratitude is promised increase while ingratitude meets severe punishment, the relation enacted by the section's abundance-and-loss examples.
The garden owner's fruit is destroyed and he wrings his hands over the collapsed trellises, a concrete reversal of fruit as secure wealth.
A fruit-bearing garden needed by an elderly owner with weak dependents is consumed by a fiery whirlwind, dramatizing the loss of sustaining produce.
The garden owners resolve to exclude the poor from the harvest, reversing the command to give produce its due at harvest in 6:141.
Rain makes the earth's growth luxuriant until its possessors feel secure, then it is made like a harvested field overnight.
Worldly life is vegetation raised by rain and then scattered dry by the wind, setting edible growth within impermanence.
After the vegetation image, lasting good deeds are declared better with the Lord in reward and hope.
Worldly growth pleases its cultivators, then yellows and crumbles, while the ayah turns to forgiveness and divine pleasure in the Hereafter.
The afterlife and worldly aims are figured as two harvests; the first is increased while the second leaves no share in the Hereafter.
People prefer the nearer life, the transient side of the section's two-world provision.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting, completing the boundary introduced by preference for the nearer life.
God expands and restricts provision, while delight in worldly life is judged slight beside the Hereafter.
Immediately after the command to eat provision from the earth, the hearer is asked whether he feels secure from that earth swallowing him.
The provision scene is further bounded by the question whether anyone is secure from a stone-bearing wind.
The water sent from heaven supplies drink and grows the vegetation on which herds feed, opening the rain-to-olive sequence of 16:11.
Water is sent down in due measure and lodged in the earth, beginning the sequence that culminates in edible gardens and the Sinai oil tree.
The food inspection is unpacked first as God's abundant pouring of water.
The earth is then split open, the physical act that makes the food list possible.
Grain is the first food grown in the sequence that later names olive.
Grapes and fresh herbage broaden the foods surrounding olive in the same catalogue.
Dense gardens provide the cultivated setting for the food list.
Fruit and pasture gather human food and animal feed in the same provision scene.
The catalogue is identified as provision for people and their livestock.
Revived dead earth produces grain from which people eat, opening a rain-and-food sequence parallel to the olive catalogues.
Palm and grape gardens with springs supply the immediate setting for eating their fruit.
Blessed rain from heaven grows gardens and harvest grain, beginning the passage that calls these foods provision.
Tall palms with layered clusters supply the fruit detail before the passage names provision.
The disciples ask whether a table can be sent down from heaven, opening a direct counterpart to the section's table and descending-food images.
They explain that they wish to eat from the heavenly table and gain reassurance and certainty.
God promises to send the table but attaches an exceptional warning to denial afterward, marking responsibility that follows provision.
Joseph orders years of sowing and preservation of grain in its ears, showing food deliberately stored to sustain people through scarcity.
The severe years consume what was stored, furnishing the famine side of the press-and-abundance scene completed in 12:49.
Quraysh's settled covenant or accustomed security opens the short passage that joins caravan journeys to feeding and safety.
The winter and summer caravan journeys supply the travel setting for the food and security named two ayat later.
The command to worship the Lord of this House identifies the giver and sanctuary behind Quraysh's food and safety.
Abraham asks that this city be secure, supplying the safety half of the fruit-provision prayer in 14:37.
The House is made a place of return and security immediately before Abraham asks for the town's fruit provision.
The House is linked with clear signs and safety for whoever enters it, reinforcing the sanctuary side of the safe-city provision image.
The source definition says the fig is eaten رَطْبًا وَيَابِسًا; this ayah's different use of moist and dry encompasses both states among what is hidden yet fully known.
Mary is told to shake the palm and receives fresh ripe dates, a direct Quranic scene of fresh fruit becoming immediate food.
Sea game is made food and benefit for residents and travelers, giving a concrete Quranic form to provisions carried on a journey.
Fire is made a reminder and a benefit for desert travelers, echoing both the olive oil's light-use and the section's caravan provision, though the fuel tree is not identified as olive.
Spending is neither wasteful nor stingy but قَوَامًا between them, applying the q-w-m idea to a measure of expenditure that sustains life.
The description of household maintainers as قَوَّامُونَ is explicitly tied to spending wealth, another q-w-m form in a material-support relation.
God places livelihoods on earth for people and for creatures they do not themselves provide for.
God's treasuries are inexhaustible while what is sent down comes in a known measure, clarifying source and measure within earthly provision.
God apportions people's livelihood in worldly life, making sustenance a distributed measure rather than a self-produced possession.
Believers are commanded to eat the good things God provided and to thank Him, matching the section's movement from food to grateful recognition.
Mary receives unexpected provision in the sanctuary, and the scene states that God provides without account.
The promised Garden contains every kind of fruit together with forgiveness, another explicit meeting of fruit and final recompense.
Abundant fruit in Paradise is given for its inhabitants to eat, treating fruit as continuing eschatological provision.
The people of Paradise have fruit and whatever they request, a concise fruit-as-reward scene.
The fruit clusters of the lofty Garden are brought near to the recipient of the record in his right hand.
The blessed are told to eat and drink for what they sent ahead, explicitly naming the meal as recompense.
The mindful receive the fruits they desire.
They are told to eat and drink in satisfaction because of what they used to do.
The passage identifies that food as God's recompense for those who do good.
The owners of a garden who swear to harvest it are presented as a trial, opening a reversal of confidence in produce.
A visitation from the Lord strikes the garden while its owners sleep, removing the crop they assumed they controlled.
After the crop's loss and their confession, the owners hope their Lord will replace it with something better.
The section's dictionary note names an olive-oil presser and seller; this immediate neighbour to the olive-lamp ayah mentions trade and sale, although it does not identify the goods as oil.
The people of Paradise call there for every kind of fruit while secure, joining fruit, safety, and final provision in one scene.
Solomon is told that God's gift is his to bestow, فَامْنُنْ, or withhold without account; the ayah joins the m-n-n gift sense to abundance without reckoning.
The messengers are commanded to eat good things and do righteous deeds, directly linking food to the deeds that receive the section's unending reward.
Whoever is mindful of God is provided for from an unexpected source, and reliance rests on God's fulfillment and measured ordering.
The inhabitants of Eden call for abundant fruit and drink, supplying the concrete feast later described in 38:54 as provision without depletion.
The people of the Garden are told to eat and drink for what they used to do, explicitly identifying the meal as recompense.
God continually supplies the Garden's people with fruit and meat they desire, completing the reward-meal of the passage.
The earth is described as bearing fruit and date palms, another direct catalogue of edible gifts.
Husked grain and fragrant plants accompany the fruit and palms of the preceding ayah, completing a table of earth-grown provision.
The two gardens contain two kinds of every fruit, presenting fruit as abundant final provision.
Fruit, palms, and pomegranates occur together in the later pair of gardens, recalling the produce catalogues in which olive and pomegranate are paired.
Chosen fruit forms part of the served banquet of the foremost, another meeting of fruit and eschatological reward.
The Garden's fruit clusters are brought within easy reach, making fruit a readily available reward rather than a failing supply.
Gardens and grapevines are the first concrete items in the reward promised to the mindful in the preceding ayah.
Water sent from heaven brings forth fruits of varied colors, a direct rain-to-fruit parallel to the olive passages.
Adjacent plots, vineyards, crops, and palms drink the same water yet differ in produce, sharpening the section's cited contrast between similar and dissimilar fruits.
The hearer is asked who sends rain and grows splendid gardens whose trees humans could not grow themselves.
Abraham names God as the one who feeds him and gives him drink, identifying the giver behind every form of sustenance.
Joseph equips his brothers with their provisions and promises full measure, a concrete caravan scene of food supplied for travel.
Joseph orders the travelers' merchandise returned to their saddlebags so they will recognize it at home and return, continuing the provisioned-caravan scene.
God brings fire from a green tree, a close counterpart to olive oil becoming light and to fuel supplied from a tree.
The hearer is asked to consider the fire people kindle, opening the tree-and-traveler benefit completed in 56:72-73.
The question asks whether people produced the fire's tree or God did, supplying the tree source for the travelers' benefit of the next ayah.
Some people count their submission as a favor to the Prophet, while the ayah says God favors them by guidance; this clarifies human reproach versus divine favor within the m-n-n root.
God says He bestowed favor upon Moses and Aaron, a m-n-n use of divine favor in the same Mosaic setting as manna and the Mount.
The ruined gardens are identified as repayment for ingratitude, making explicit why the provision of 34:15 was reversed.
Between Saba and the blessed towns, God placed visible settlements and measured stages, telling the people to travel through them safely by night and day.
The people ask that their journeys be lengthened, wrong themselves, and are scattered, reversing the safe and measured travel provision of 34:18.
The garden parable begins with two vineyards surrounded by palms and crops, establishing the fruit wealth later destroyed.
Both gardens yield all their fruit without failing and have a river between them, defining the abundance reversed in 18:42.
Believers are told to eat the lawful good things God provided and remain mindful of Him, joining food, provision, and moral response.
Adam is promised that in the Garden he will neither hunger nor be unclothed, defining sustenance by the needs it continuously removes.
The Garden also protects Adam from thirst and exposure to the sun, completing the picture of provision that keeps a human being whole.
God expands and restricts provision, replaces whatever is spent, and is called the best provider.
Spending is scaled to the provision one has received, and restricted provision still carries a command to spend from God's gift.
Every creature's provision is God's responsibility, making sustaining livelihood universal rather than confined to the foods named in the section.
The seven green ears and seven dry ears echo the source definition's fresh/dry wording within the famine-and-provision story, though the objects are grain rather than figs.

The wording can mean not to confer a favor seeking increase; on that reading it contrasts interested human giving with the section's unceasing divine reward, though the verb's interpretation is disputed.
